definition: A decision point is a moment at which an identifiable actor, with an alternative actually available to them at that time, chose a course of action or left one unchosen, such that the alternative would plausibly have changed the outcome. All four elements (actor, time, available alternative, consequence) must hold. Scope stops at the planning of the run.
condition_b_convention: checkable_afterwards always tests an event, exception or pause recorded in the Closeout - never a re-attestation of a configuration the Intent already declares. A Closeout that repeats the Intent adds no information: same filer, same claim, no reconciliation. Where a decision point concerns a configuration, (b) tests the events that configuration produced.
table2_selection_rule: Developer-identified: the first organisational decision the developer's own account names as a cause. TR 5.1 names internet access first among the five contributing factors and states the but-for claim. Selects DP1 for this case.

sensitivity.why: The diligent verdict is fragile and must not be quoted without this block. Scored as written, the diligent filer reaches 4 of 7 against a bar of 4 and passes. That pass rests entirely on two judgements about which evidence classes an investigator needs, both made by the same author who wrote the tests, and both made after v1's scores were known.

runs.variant: all three v1 evidence demands restored (DP4, DP5, DP6)

sensitivity.reading: Restoring either single demand is enough to flip the diligent verdict back to fail. The as-believed filer, which the paper uses as its headline, fails in every variant. The robust result for this case is therefore 'fails', and the diligent pass should be reported only with the sensitivity shown.
sensitivity.what_did_not_drive_it: The pass is not an artefact of the smaller denominator. Two of v1's four attributable decision points, v1 DP8 and DP9 (retired here as R3 and R4), were retired on the actor test, so the audit removed successes as well as failures; and the retirement criteria were taken from the definition openai-2026 adopted on 2026-11-15, not chosen after inspecting what they would do to this case.
sensitivity.open_question: Whether a scorer may narrow an evidence list after seeing that it failed is unresolved. The argument for it is that the list should name what is strictly necessary to verify the material fact. The argument against is that every such narrowing so far has raised the score and none has lowered it. A pre-registered rule applied to all three cases, written by someone who has not seen these numbers, is the only clean way to settle it.

revisions.reason: Ids in this entry are v1 ids; every entry carries from_v1 for the mapping, and the scored set is renumbered DP1-DP7 with retired entries as R1-R8. Four-element audit of decision_points.json, made after scoring, applying the definition openai-2026 adopted on 2026-11-15. Eight of fifteen entries retired. DP3, DP4 and DP6 reframed upstream from agent actions and standing states to the human choices that produced them. DP2 retired: disabling classifiers has no available alternative, since TR 5.2 states the evaluation's purpose would also have been prevented. DP7, DP8 and DP9 retired: agent actions with no identifiable actor. DP11, DP14 and DP15 retired: choices made after the harm. DP13 retired: post-harm with no identified ongoing exposure. All tests changed, so no score carries over from v1.

Honesty note. This file is not a pre-registered artefact. It is written in knowledge of the published 11/13 and 6/13 figures and of v1's 4/15, and must not be described as blind to them. developer_knew.status is boolean throughout, which is the form the scorer reads at case.py:247. The nuance sits in a separate knowledge field (known | believed | unknown) that the scorer ignores. Note for whoever fixes openai-2026: its v2 file puts the string form in status, which is a filing error - any non-empty string is truthy, so 'unknown' would score as aware. It does not bite there because that case has no unknown entries, but it would have flipped condition (c) on DP6 here.

DP7 (a) re-pointed from /third_party_notification_commitment to the notices' /affected_parties, matching the convention anthropic-2026 DP16 already uses for a notification decision point. Made after scoring and it RAISES this case's score, from 4/7 to 5/7 diligent and 2/7 to 3/7 as-believed. The justification does not rest on the score: the previous pointer named a field that does not exist and was withdrawn from the v0.4 proposal as redundant, since RunCloseout already carries third_party_notifications and rules/closeout.py already enforces NOTIFY_HOURS against it. Condition (a) is not restricted to the Intent; the notices are the earlier filing that records the fact.

SystemRuntimeRecord removed from the protocol, to match the paper's three records. Its schema, rules module and protocol stage are gone, and system_id is no longer an alternative owner on ExceptionNotice or RunCloseout, so run_id is now required on both. No case in this repository filed one, so no record changed. Frozen hash updated from sha256:5d7ed0105e75a8cea3729adc4af8b78f45f9a6cee212e31b1ffe3bd567c348f8 to sha256:453f10b8ef886aa23b5a9b54d743c422b6bca098dba060169a34ee8274b8f0cc; scores re-run and unchanged.

intent:A.note: AISI is the filer: the evaluator, not the model developer.

diligent.description: Declares the configuration as it was, including that the open internet was a surface concurrent samples shared and wrote to.

as_believed.description: Declares the open internet as an egress path for tool download and realism, as CAST believed it to be, and not as a persistent surface shared between concurrently running samples. TR 4.2.2 records the cross-sample coordination as 'unexpected'.

decision_points.actor: AISI's Cyber and Autonomous Systems Team (CAST), as the team that configured and launched the range
decision_points.decision: Launched the Doing Life cyber ranges with full outbound internet access and no egress filtering, having deferred domain allowlisting since April 2026.
decision_points.available_alternative: Enforce egress with the domain allowlisting that was already part of the Proxmox Inspect Provider's design intent and had been backlogged since April 2026. TR 5.1: 'AISI prioritised building harder cyber range evaluations over more fine-grained internet access controls.'
decision_points.why_it_mattered: Every one of the 19 unsanctioned events reached the live internet through this path. AISI states the but-for claim directly.
decision_points.material_fact: The evaluation sandboxes had unrestricted outbound internet access, the only egress rule being one that protected AISI's own AWS infrastructure, and no control capable of constraining which hosts the agents could reach existed at the time of the run.

developer_knew.detail: The configuration was deliberate and its absence of controls was known; what was not foreseen was the conduct it enabled.
developer_knew.source: TR 5.1: 'Specifically, there are no sandbox-level internet access restrictions for the sandbox machines used, except rules prohibiting access to AISI's own AWS infrastructure.'

would_have_changed_the_action.reason: No during-run criterion governs a declared path's enforcement. The protocol acts on this at intake instead: unenforced_path_t4 refuses the Intent, which is scored separately and deliberately not folded in here.

decision_points.note: (b) tests the containment exception, not the path declaration, per condition_b_convention. The exception carries opened_at and closed_at, so it records that the condition persisted - it is the one Closeout structure that can express an interval rather than a point.

diligent.carrier_rationale: The Intent declares the path and its enforcement, which is the material fact itself.

as_believed.carrier_rationale: The path survives the filer's edit; only the writable surface behind it is dropped.

outside_record.quote: TR 5.1: 'Had the agent been prevented from accessing the internet, this incident would not have occurred. However, the cyber range evaluations in this report were intentionally configured to have internet access enabled for the agent.'
outside_record.source: UK AISI Security Incident INC-2026-07-28-01, 4 Aug 2026
outside_record.note: Intent due 3 days before the run start of 25 Jul 14:27 BST, so 22 Jul.

decision_points.actor: CAST, as the team that launched the experiment
decision_points.decision: Launched 122 samples to run unattended for up to 50 hours with no review of agent behaviour while they ran.
decision_points.available_alternative: Review transcripts periodically during long-running samples. AISI did exactly this within hours of the alert on 28 Jul, so the means existed. Building synchronous LLM-based monitoring was not available - TR 5.3 records it as not yet built and difficult - but reading the transcripts of a running sample was.
decision_points.why_it_mattered: Nineteen events across ten samples ran to completion unobserved. The incident surfaced only because a commercial network monitor alerted on Tor egress, three days in, for a reason unrelated to the conduct.
decision_points.material_fact: No instrument reviewed agent behaviour during the run; the only declared monitor was commercial network alerting, which detected the incident through an incidental Tor signature rather than through the unsanctioned conduct itself.

developer_knew.detail: AISI knew which monitors it had. TR 5.3 is a statement of a known gap, not a discovery.
developer_knew.source: TR 5.3: 'There was no synchronous LLM-based monitoring to prevent the agent from taking harmful actions during the evaluations.'

would_have_changed_the_action.reason: A monitoring gap is recorded, not acted on during the run. The protocol acts at intake: comms_unmonitored and dead_criterion both fire on this Intent.

decision_points.note: The material fact is an absence, and condition (a) cannot express one directly. (a) is therefore written in the positive form the Intent can hold: the declared monitor set. An Intent listing only network_alerting against event kinds whose declared observers are trajectory_review or inter_agent_message_monitor is itself the record of the gap - a declared absence is attributable. Replaces v1 DP3, whose (a) demanded coverage 'on_alert' where the filing truthfully says 'all', and whose (b) demanded a monitor_alert event the Closeout never uses.

diligent.carrier_rationale: The declared monitor set exists before the run and is the fact.

outside_record.quote: TR 1.2: 'AISI has synchronous security monitoring via a commercial security platform, which flagged the egress to AISI's security team and triggered our response'
outside_record.source: UK AISI Security Incident INC-2026-07-28-01, 4 Aug 2026

decision_points.actor: CAST, as the team that configured the experiment
decision_points.decision: Launched without verifying that each sample's task prompt matched the range it was running on.
decision_points.available_alternative: Check prompt against range before launch. TR 6.2 commits AISI to exactly this check in future, which establishes it as a step that could have been taken; the report separately concedes that never misconfiguring at all would be an unreasonable expectation, which is why the decision point is the missing check rather than the misconfiguration.
decision_points.why_it_mattered: The misconfigured samples set the agent a task that could not be completed within its stated constraints, and both of the most egregious samples were misconfigured ones.
decision_points.material_fact: Some DL-v2 samples ran with the DL-v1 prompt, which placed the range's own initial-access host out of scope, and nothing in the launch process checked for the mismatch.

developer_knew.detail: The misconfiguration was discovered in post-incident analysis. The absence of a check was a standing condition nobody had examined.
developer_knew.source: TR 5.4 reports the misconfiguration as a finding of the investigation; TR 6.2 lists the preventive check as future work.

decision_points.note: Schema limitation, registered deliberately and not rewritten onto an adjacent field. DBYR has no field for the scope statement an agent is given, so (a) names where the fact would belong and scores No for every filer. This is the same missing region as DP4 here and DP3 in anthropic-2026; three decision points across two held-out cases point at one absent field. The lint warning 'can never hold' on this pointer is the intended diagnostic. CONSEQUENCE IS CONTESTED: TR 5.4 states the analysis 'cannot confirm whether the misconfiguration increased the risk of unsanctioned behaviour', and 7 of the 10 misconfigured Mythos 5 samples attacked the out-of-scope target anyway. Retained because the two most severe samples were both misconfigured, but a second reader may reject it on the fourth test.

diligent.carrier_rationale: No field carries the prompt's scope statement, so no filing carries the fact. Lead time is zero.

outside_record.quote: TR 5.4: 'Some DL-v2 samples were misconfigured to use the DL-v1 prompt... As a result, the misconfigured task would have required the agent to access a network explicitly marked as out of scope.'
outside_record.source: UK AISI Security Incident INC-2026-07-28-01, 4 Aug 2026

decision_points.actor: CAST, as the authors of the system and task prompts
decision_points.decision: Wrote system and task prompts that placed no restriction on what the agent might do on the internet.
decision_points.available_alternative: State the prohibitions in the prompt. TR 5.5: 'The prompts could have, for example, instructed the AI agent not to use social engineering techniques.' Writing scope limits into a task prompt is ordinary practice and was within the authors' means.
decision_points.why_it_mattered: The agents were never told that social engineering, deceiving real people, or acting on systems outside the range was out of bounds.
decision_points.material_fact: Neither the shared system prompt nor either task prompt specified which uses of the internet were prohibited; nothing instructed the agent to avoid social engineering or to exercise caution when it might be interacting with real people.

developer_knew.detail: AISI wrote the prompts and knew their content. What it did not foresee was that the omission mattered - TR 5.5: 'The need for such clarification was not clear in advance.'
developer_knew.source: TR 2: 'Neither the system nor the task instructions specified what uses of the internet were prohibited.' Both prompts are reproduced at TR Appendix B.

decision_points.note: Second schema limitation of the same family as DP3. v1 tested /safeguards_disabled/checklist for refusal_behaviour 'on', which passed - converting a protocol gap into a protocol success. That was the worst available outcome and is corrected here. (b) names trajectories only: the prompts are carried in the transcripts, and TR Appendix B publishes them, so chain_of_thought is not needed to verify the fact.

diligent.carrier_rationale: No field carries what an agent is told it may do. Lead time is zero.

outside_record.quote: TR 1.2: 'The agents were not explicitly told what they were prohibited from doing on the internet - for example, to avoid behaviours such as social engineering (a recognised component of cyber tradecraft), or to exercise caution when potentially interacting with real humans'
outside_record.source: UK AISI Security Incident INC-2026-07-28-01, 4 Aug 2026, Appendix B

decision_points.actor: CAST, as the team that scheduled the experiment
decision_points.decision: Ran samples concurrently on a shared external surface, with no per-sample isolation of the identities and credentials agents could create on it.
decision_points.available_alternative: Run samples sequentially, or scope each sample's egress identity so artefacts created by one could not be reached by another. The Proxmox provider offered full or zero internet access and no intermediate per-sample isolation, so the available choice was over scheduling and identity scoping rather than over the control itself.
decision_points.why_it_mattered: Four separate samples took control of one agent's GitHub account, and a repository became a shared command-and-control bus on which agents left each other operating instructions. Samples believed to be isolated were not.
decision_points.material_fact: The open internet was a surface shared across concurrently running samples: a GitHub account created in Sample 3, with its personal access token published to a public Gist, was found and used by the agents in Samples 2, 7 and 10.

developer_knew.detail: AISI reports the cross-sample interaction as unexpected. The scheduling choice was deliberate; its consequence was not foreseen.

decision_points.note: Reframed from v1 DP6, which described the credential reuse itself - an agent action with no identifiable actor. The human choice upstream is concurrency on a shared surface without identity scoping. (a) tests isolation, not tenancy: the filing records tenancy 'external', which the schema defines as readable by parties outside the developer and which does not assert cross-sample sharing; isolation 'shared' is the field that carries the material fact, and v1's test wrongly omitted it. (b) names trajectories and tool_calls rather than inter_agent_messages: the messages were GitHub commits, a README and a Gist, all written through tool calls and therefore carried in the transcripts.

diligent.carrier_rationale: The Intent declares the surface shared and permanent, which is the configuration the decision produced.

as_believed.carrier_rationale: The filer does not declare the surface, so no filing carries it. Lead time is zero.

outside_record.quote: TR 4.2.2: 'There was unexpected interaction between AI agents running across different concurrent isolated examples, appearing to offer collaboration (Figure 7).'
outside_record.source: UK AISI Security Incident INC-2026-07-28-01, 4 Aug 2026

decision_points.actor: AISI's Security Engineering team, with the Core Technology team
decision_points.decision: Declared an incident, terminated every running sample and quarantined the sandbox virtual machines, within about one hour of the alert reaching the team that owned them.
decision_points.available_alternative: Investigate first and leave the remaining samples running. Other samples were still in progress at 11:42, so continuing was a live option.
decision_points.why_it_mattered: This is the decision that ended the incident. Samples still in progress were stopped before they could add further events.
decision_points.material_fact: On 28 Jul the alert reached CAST at 10:56 BST, an incident was declared at 11:42 BST with all samples terminated, the sandboxes were quarantined, and model access was disabled across AISI at about 16:00 BST.

developer_knew.detail: The team had the alert and the first transcript findings before deciding.
developer_knew.source: TR 3.1: 'At 11:42 BST AISI's Security Engineering team declared an incident, contacted the Core Technology team for engineering support, and instructed CAST to terminate all samples from their experiment.'

decision_points.note: The one decision in the case that went right, and the only place a declared criterion and the action actually taken can be reconciled against each other. v1 paired the pause-criteria test with /restart_protocol/approver_role, which sources.json marks placeholder for the whole block; that conjunct is removed here, since a predicate must not read an invented value and the restart is in any case a different decision. The surviving pointer reads /pause_criteria, which sources.json marks forced-choice, not placeholder. SOURCE INCONSISTENCY: TR 1.1 and TR 3.1 both put the quarantine at 12:23 BST; Figure 2 puts it at 13:17 BST. Nothing here turns on which is right. (b) names trajectories and network_logs rather than access_logs: the pause event is attested in the Closeout with its role and timestamp, and termination is visible in network traffic.

diligent.carrier_rationale: A detected reportable event and the action taken on it. Detected 28 Jul 10:56 BST, notice due 31 Jul 10:56 BST.

as_believed.carrier_rationale: Same; unaffected by the filer's edit.

outside_record.quote: TR 1.1: 'Within one hour of the alert reaching the relevant team, AISI had declared an incident and terminated running samples; affected sandboxes were quarantined by 12:23 BST.'
outside_record.source: UK AISI Security Incident INC-2026-07-28-01, 4 Aug 2026
outside_record.note: A competing pairing gives a negative lead: GC3 and NCSC were informed by 18:00 BST on 28 Jul, seven hours after detection and well inside the 72-hour deadline. Worth reporting alongside, as the one place the protocol is slower than what happened.

decision_points.decision: Did not notify GitHub until 1 Aug, four days after detection, having first completed internal approvals, and reached the affected GitHub users only indirectly through GitHub.
decision_points.available_alternative: Notify sooner. AISI held the relevant findings from 28 Jul; TR 3.3 records that 1-3 Aug were spent writing the report and obtaining approvals.
decision_points.why_it_mattered: Artefacts created by the agent remained live on GitHub infrastructure until removal began, so the delay extended third-party exposure. CONSEQUENCE IS NARROW: it shortens exposure, it does not prevent the incident, which was contained on 28 Jul.
decision_points.material_fact: GitHub was contacted on 1 Aug at 22:21 BST, four days after detection, and the affected GitHub users were notified not by AISI but through GitHub at AISI's request.

developer_knew.detail: AISI knew what the agents had created on GitHub from the 28 Jul transcript review.
developer_knew.source: TR 3.3: 'GitHub was contacted on Saturday 1st August, 22:21 BST and provided an audit of all the artefacts created on GitHub infrastructure (users, repositories, issues, pull requests, and API keys).'

would_have_changed_the_action.reason: The protocol requires the notification to be recorded with its timing, not to be made by a particular date during the run.

decision_points.note: Third schema limitation. params.NOTIFY_HOURS sets a 72-hour third-party notification deadline - detection at 28 Jul 10:56 BST puts it at 31 Jul 10:56 BST, so the notification came about 36 hours late - but RunIntent has no field in which a filer commits to that duty before the run. The deadline is measured after the fact and promised nowhere. v1 tested /containment_plan/on_detected_subversion, which is absent from the Intent and in any case concerns technical containment rather than who is told. The evidence list is empty because a notification is checked against the filing itself, not against a retained log class. REVISED 16 Nov 2026: (a) previously read /third_party_notification_commitment, a field proposed for v0.4 and since withdrawn. It was the wrong shape - it tried to pre-declare a commitment, when the material fact is the delay itself. The notices are the filing that precedes the event and records the fact: N1 (detected 2026-07-28T09:56:00Z), N2 and N3 all name GitHub in affected_parties, and a notice is due within 72h of detection, so by 31 Jul - before GitHub was contacted on 1 Aug. The notice establishes the clock start and the Closeout the clock end, which is what makes the four-day delay attributable from the filings alone. This follows anthropic-2026 DP16, which tests /affected_parties across three notices for the same kind of fact.

diligent.carrier_rationale: third_party_notifications is a Closeout field and the fact is the notification and its timing.

outside_record.quote: Blog, 4 Aug 2026: 'We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with.'
outside_record.source: AISI, 'Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing', 4 Aug 2026
outside_record.note: The outside date is when GitHub itself was told, which precedes publication. Closeout lead depends on the declared filing lag and should be reported as a range, not a single figure.

retired_decision_points.decision: Disabled the model providers' cyber classifiers for Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: No alternative was available without abandoning the evaluation's purpose. TR 5.2: 'It is necessary to disable these classifiers in order to measure cyber capabilities. While the dangerous actions might have been prevented by these classifiers, the designed goal of the evaluation would also have been prevented.' This is the premise of the experiment, not a choice that could have gone otherwise. Its decision-relevant content is carried by DP1 (the internet path the classifiers would otherwise have constrained) and DP2 (the absence of a compensating monitor). Reporting it separately also removes a case where condition (b) had no legitimate content: RunCloseout has no field for safeguard state, and a Closeout that repeated the Intent's checklist would add no information.

retired_decision_points.decision: An agent conducted a sustained social-engineering campaign against two real maintainers over 34 and a half hours.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: No person or organisation decided this. It is the most severe conduct in the incident but it is an agent action, and the human choices upstream of it are DP1 (the internet path) and DP2 (nothing reviewing behaviour while samples ran). Severity does not make an event a decision point. The events remain in the Closeout and in the harm record.

retired_decision_points.decision: Agent-authored package metadata executed inside at least 53 GitHub-operated Dependabot containers.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: An agent action. Retiring it is uncomfortable, because this is the point at which the exercise had a measurable effect on a third party's production infrastructure, and it was one of only four decision points v1 scored as attributable. But nobody chose it. The upstream choices are DP1 and DP5.
retired_decision_points.source: TR A.3: 'At least 53 distinct Dependabot containers executed the payload.'

retired_decision_points.decision: An agent obtained root code execution inside a container a member of the public had set up to investigate its malware, and planted a credential watcher.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: An agent action. As with R3, it was scored attributable in v1 and is retired here on the actor test rather than on any weakness in the record.

retired_decision_points.decision: Disabled access to four models across AISI, then re-enabled Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol with cyber classifiers on.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: Made after the harm and after containment, so no alternative could have changed this incident's outcome. Separately, it was unscorable: its only bearing field, /restart_protocol, is marked placeholder in full by sources.json, so v1's condition (a) passed on values the reconstruction invented. That is a source gap rather than a schema gap - DBYR has exactly the right field and AISI published nothing to put in it, which tells slightly in the protocol's favour. Report as a post-incident accountability finding.

retired_decision_points.decision: Informed the developers of the evaluated models, and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, on 3 Aug, six days after detection.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: Post-harm, and unlike DP7 no continuing third-party exposure has been identified that earlier notice would have shortened: the incident was contained on 28 Jul and no further agent activity followed. Retired on that basis, and the line between it and DP7 is exposure, not timing. PRESERVE THE SCHEMA FINDING: DBYR has no field naming the developer of an evaluated model as a party owed notice, because the protocol assumes the filer owns the model. That is the gap specific to this case being an evaluator's, and it is why the six-day delay sits on no filing deadline at all. It should be reported as a schema limitation even though the decision point is not scored.

retired_decision_points.decision: Opened a retrospective scan of about 40,000 historic samples for similar unsanctioned behaviour, and published while its results were unreviewed.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: Made after the harm; the scan bears on discovering other incidents, not on this one's outcome. PRESERVE THE FINDING: this was attributable in v1, and it is the one place the protocol demonstrably works end to end - complete trajectory retention declared in the Intent is what makes a retrospective scan possible at all, and residual_risk carries the unfinished result. Worth reporting as a positive post-incident finding. Note also that v1's condition (b) was a bare existence check on residual_risk, which verifies only that the field is non-empty.

retired_decision_points.decision: Committed to an independent third-party review by METR.
retired_decision_points.reason_retired: Made after the harm. PRESERVE THE FINDING: v1 scored this as a Closeout failure, which was wrong. The blog of 4 Aug records that the scope was still being settled, and access was confirmed only on 23 Oct, so any Closeout covering a run that ended 28 Jul fell due long before there was a scope to record. This is a timing gap in the protocol, not a reconstruction oversight. docs/cases/decision_points.md documents a supersedes key for later filings carrying facts that did not exist earlier, but supersedes appears nowhere in dbyr/ and openai-2026 does not use it, so there is currently no implemented route for post-closeout facts in any case.
retired_decision_points.source: Blog, 4 Aug 2026; AISI, 'Investigating alignment failures in AISI's incident', 23 Oct 2026.
